label: Sharp edges
summary: Sheet metal edges, cut wires, blades and broken plastic cause deep cuts. With no medical care, an infected cut can become life-threatening.
signs: Cut or punched sheet metal: computer cases, ducting, appliance panels
Blades in shredders, blenders, mowers and fans
Snapped plastic, cut wire ends and cut cable ties
Rusty metal, hidden screws and nails in rubble
do: Wear gloves for all teardown work
File or tape cut edges as you make them
Cut away from your body and keep your other hand behind the blade
Look before you reach into a cavity
dont: Don't run your hand along an edge to feel it
Don't reach blind into bins, cabinets or cushions
Don't hold a part in your hand while cutting it
Don't leave cut metal lying where people walk
ppe: Cut-resistant gloves (EN 388 or ANSI A-rated); leather alone isn’t cut-resistant
No gloves near spinning machines: they can pull a hand in
Long sleeves, and boots with puncture-resistant soles (PR, the CSA green triangle, S3)
firstAid: Press firmly on the cut with a clean pad for at least 10 minutes
Rinse well with clean water that was boiled and cooled, and cover with a clean dressing
Change the dressing daily; spreading redness, heat, pus, red streaks or fever need medical care
Deep, gaping or dirty cuts, or cuts with numbness or weak movement, need medical care
Dirty or rusty wounds carry a tetanus risk; get a booster if any medical help exists

Blood spurting or soaking through pad after pad on an arm or leg: keep pressing hard; if it won't stop, tie a wide strip of cloth tight 5–8 cm above the cut, not on a joint, twist it with a stick until bleeding stops, note the time and leave it on
Don't pull out a large or deeply stuck piece of metal or glass: pad around it, keep it still and get medical help
